text: Earlier in this path you learned the shared responsibility model: the provider owns security OF the cloud, and you own security IN the cloud. That split doesn't change for compliance — it just gets read differently. It tells you exactly which half of any audit belongs to AWS or Microsoft, and which half belongs entirely to you.

Security OF the cloud — the datacenter, the hypervisor, the network backbone — is always the provider's audit scope. Security IN the cloud — your access controls, your encryption settings, your logging configuration — is always your audit scope. No matter how the provider is certified, that second half never transfers to them.

Take a healthcare startup running on Azure. Azure holds a real SOC 2 Type II report and ISO 27001 certification, covering its own datacenters, hypervisor, and network. It's tempting for the startup to tell a customer "we're compliant because we're on Azure" and stop there. But when an auditor actually reviews the startup itself, they ask for the startup's own access control list, its encryption-at-rest configuration, and its log retention policy — none of which Azure's certificate says anything about, because those are configuration decisions the startup made, not Microsoft.

That doesn't mean you start from zero every audit cycle. Compliance inheritance lets your own auditor accept the provider's audited report as proof for the infrastructure layer, treating Azure or AWS as what SOC 2 calls a sub-service organization, instead of re-testing a hyperscaler's datacenter floor from scratch. You still need to actually produce that report when asked, though. AWS publishes its own through AWS Artifact, a self-service portal built into the console. Microsoft publishes Azure's equivalent through the Microsoft Service Trust Portal — pull it from there directly, not from a support ticket.

Next lesson: SOC 2 and ISO 27001, applied specifically to how you configure and operate your own cloud environment — the same access controls, encryption, logging, and incident response you've already built, now framed as the actual evidence an audit asks to see.
